pages.title: Welcome to the Git course!
pages.content:
* Imagine you’re working on a project in **VS Code**.
* You’ve been coding for hours — things are working fine. You keep pressing **Ctrl + S** to save your progress.
* Then you make a few more changes, tweak a function, or rename a variable… and suddenly, the project breaks.
* You wish you could go back to that perfect version from 30 minutes ago, but you can’t.

**That’s where **Git** comes in.**


---

**In this course, you’ll learn how Git helps you:**

* Take **snapshots** of your code (called **commits**)
* **See** what changed and when
* **Restore** any older version easily
* **Collaborate** with others without overwriting their work

It’s like having **Ctrl + Z** that never forgets, even after you shut down your laptop.

callout.text: Git records project history as commits and separates working-directory changes from staged and committed snapshots.

pages.title: Understanding How Git Works
pages.content:
- Now that Git knows who you are, you’re ready to start using Git and actually track your projects.
- When we talk about how Git works, we come across three components — Working Directory, Staging Area, and Repository.


---

**Three Components**


- **Working Directory**: The working directory is the project folder on your system where your actual files and code exist.
Any new files you create or changes you make happen here first.

- **Staging Area**: The staging area is a temporary storage inside Git where you place selected changes that you want to include in the next commit.
- **Repository**: The local repository is the hidden storage that contains the complete history of your project and all committed snapshots.


**Both staging area and local repository data are stored in the .git folder.**


--- 

**Example Scenario**

- You have three files in your VS Code / working directory on your local machine:
```bash
You edit three files:

index.html final changes
style.css ⏳ still working on it
app.js ready to save
```

- You can stage only the ready files(moved to staging area):
```bash
index.html final changes
app.js ready to save
```

- After you are sure, you can commit everything present in your staging area to the local repository.

pages.title: Version Control System (VCS)
pages.content:
- You have learned the basics of a Version Control System (VCS)
- Even though we didn’t use the term earlier, everything you learned falls under a category called: Version Control System
- **Version Control System**, a system that tracks changes in your files and lets you go back to previous versions whenever needed.
- **Git** is one of the most powerful and widely used version control systems in the world.

---

**What Next?**

- Now that you understand how Git works internally, next you will learn Git commands and workflow, including:
 - Tracking files
 - Staging changes
 - Committing changes
 - Viewing history
- In the next lessons, you’ll start using Git practically to manage real project versions.

pages.title: Initializing a Git Repository
pages.content:
In previous module, you've learned what Git is and how it works behind the scenes. \
Now it’s time to **actually start using Git**.

Imagine you’re starting a new project. \
To let Git track it -
**Open your terminal** and type:
```bash
git init
```
You’ve just created your **first Git repository**!

---

**What is a Git Repository?** \
A Git repository (repo) is where Git stores everything about your project. It :
- Keeps all versions of your files
- Lets you go back to older versions
- Helps you track changes safely
- Makes easier to collaborate with others without losing work.

---

When you run `git init`, Git creates a **hidden folder** called **`.git`** — this is where all your project’s history and data are stored. \
That’s what turns your folder into a **Git repository**.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: A reliable Git workflow is initialize, inspect status, stage intended changes, commit with a clear message, and inspect history.

pages.title: Adding Files (git add)
pages.content:
You’ve initialized your Git repository, and your folder is now being tracked.
The **next step** is to **tell Git which changes you want to include in your next commit**. \
**This is done with the `git add` command**.

---

**What is git add?**
- As we learned in the **Git workflow**, any changes you make in the working directory must first be added to the staging area before committing
- The `git add` command does exactly that — it **moves your changes from the working directory to the staging area**, preparing them for a commit.


---

**Different Ways to Add Files :** 
1. Add a single file
```bash
git add filename
```
2. Add multiple files at once
```bash
git add file1 file2 file3
```
3. Add all changes in the folder
```bash
git add .
```
This stages all new, modified, or deleted files in the **current directory**.

pages.title: Committing Changes (git commit -m)
pages.content:
You’ve added your file to the **staging area** — now it’s time to **save that change permanently in Git’s history.**
This step is called a **commit**.

---

**What is a Commit?** \
As we learned earlier in the **Git workflow**, after adding files to the **staging area**, the next step is to **commit** them — this moves your changes from the staging area to the repository.


A **commit** is like taking a snapshot of your project at that moment in time. \
It records:
- What changes were made
- When they were made
- Who made them \
Each commit gets a **unique ID**, so you can always return to that exact version later.

---

**Commit staged files** (most common) \
Use this when you’ve already added files to the staging area using git add.
```bash
git commit -m "Your commit message"
```

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: A reliable Git workflow is initialize, inspect status, stage intended changes, commit with a clear message, and inspect history.

pages.title: Git Configuration
pages.content:
Before you commit anything in git, you need to tell it **who you are** — your **name** and **email address**. \
Git uses this information - **to record who made each change in a project**. 

You can do this using the **git config command** : 

**User Name :** 
Your name will be attached to your commits
```bash
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
```
**Email Address :** \
Your email is also attached to your commits
```bash
git config --global user.email "youremail@example.com"
```

pages.title: Skip git add for Modified Files
pages.content:
If you’ve **modified existing tracked files** : 

Files that are **already in the staging area (i.e., already tracked by Git)** may be modified again later.
In such cases, you can skip running `git add` again and perform staging + commit together using:
```bash
git commit -am "Your commit message"
```
**Note**: This doesn’t include new files, they must be added first with `git add`

---

**Let's understand this from an example :** \
Let’s say you have two files — `file1.txt` and `file2.txt` — already tracked by Git (i.e they are already added in staging area).

**Now you modify only `file1.txt`** - \
Do you need to run git add again before committing? 

**Not necessarily!** \
Since `file1.txt` is already tracked, you can **skip `git add`** and directly use:
```bash
git commit -am "Update file1"
```
Here’s what happens: \
-a automatically stages all modified tracked files. \
-m adds your commit message.

**So, no need to add tracked files again — Git handles it for you!**

callout.text: A reliable Git workflow is initialize, inspect status, stage intended changes, commit with a clear message, and inspect history.

pages.title: Viewing commit history (git log, git show)
pages.content:
Now that you’ve made some commits, let’s see how to view your project’s history.


**1. `git log`** : \
Shows a list of all commits — who made them, when, and the commit messages.
```bash
git log
```
You’ll see details like: 
- Commit ID (a unique hash)
- Author (your name and email)
- Date and time
- Commit message

**2. `git show`**

Displays detailed information and code changes for a specific commit.
```bash
git show 
```
This shows the commit message, author info, and the actual code changes (diff).

pages.title: Understanding Branches in Git
pages.content:
You understand how commits record your progress — \
Now, let’s unlock Git’s real power: **branching**, where real collaboration begins.

**Why We Use Branches?** \
Imagine you’re working on a project, and you want to try adding a new feature — but you don’t want to mess up your main code. \
That’s where **branches** come in!

---

**Branches let you:**
- Work on **new features** or **bug fixes** by **creating new branch** for making new changes **without affecting the main code**.
- Experiment freely also make **collaboration** easy.
- **Switch between different versions** of your project easily.

**Visual representation of Branches:** 


**To Creates a new git branch with the specified name use:**
```bash
git branch 
```
we'll explore git commands in detail later...

pages.title: Create and Switch in One Step
pages.content:
Is it possible to use a **single command to create a new branch** and **switch** to it —
instead of running two commands like this?
```bash
git branch feature-branch
git switch feature-branch
```
**Yes, absolutely!**

**Git gives you a shortcut for this:**
```bash
git switch -c feature-branch
```
The `-c` stands for create here.

- This single command **creates a new branch named `feature-branch`** 
- **Switches to it immediately**, so you can start working right away. 


---

**Note :** \
In earlier versions of Git before `git switch` was introduced. - 
```bash
git checkout -b 
```

This older command does the same job as **`git switch -c`**, but it was used.

pages.title: Viewing and Comparing Branches
pages.content:
You’ve built your branches earlier — now it’s time to **compare** them and see their **differences**.

When working on multiple branches, you’ll often want to:
- Check **which branches exist** in your repository
- See **what’s inside each branch**
- Compare **differences** between two branches before merging \
That’s where a few helpful git commands comes:

---
**Before comparing branches**, **viewing branches** helps you confirm **which branches exist** and which one you want to compare.

**Step 1: Viewing Branches** 
```bash
git branch → To list all branches in your repository
git branch -v → To view branches along with their latest commit message and commit hash
```


---

**Step 2: Comparing Branches and Commits** \
The git diff command helps you see changes between:
- Working directory and staging area
- Two branches
- Two commits
```bash
git diff → Unstaged changes (working directory vs. last commit)
git diff --staged → Changes that are staged but not yet committed
git diff branch1 branch2 → Compare differences between two branches.
git diff commit1 commit2 → Compare changes between two commits.
```

---

These commands help you 
- **keep track of your progress** 
- **know exactly what changed** before merging.
- **Avoid conflicts before merging.**

pages.title: Getting Started with Git Merging
pages.content:
So far, we’ve learned that branches help us work on different features or experiments independently, without touching the main code. \
But **once our work is done…** \
we need to **bring those changes back together**. \
That’s where **merging** comes in.

---

**What is Merging in Git?**
- Merging in Git means **combining the changes from one branch into another**.
- This is how you **bring your work together after working separately** on different features or bug fixes.

**Visual representation of Merging:**

After merging work, your branches start to pile up. \
To keep your repository clean, you should delete branches you no longer need.

**Why Delete a Branch?** \
Because **once a feature is merged**, that branch has served its purpose. \
**Keeping unused branches only creates confusion**.

```bash
git branch -d branch-name
```

**Git will stop you from deleting** if the branch still has **unmerged work**.

---

**Force Delete :**
```bash
git branch -D branch-name
```
This deletes the branch even if it has unmerged changes. \
**Use only when you're sure you don’t need the work on that branch**.

pages.title: Undoing & Ignoring Changes
pages.content:
When working with Git, mistakes are normal — adding the wrong file, changing something accidentally, or committing too early.
This submodule teaches you how to **fix mistakes safely** and how to **ignore files that should not be tracked**.

Think of this module as your **“Git safety kit”**— it helps you stay confident while working.

---

**Ignoring Files with `.gitignore` :** \
Not every file in your project should go into Git. 

**Examples:**
- `node_modules/`
- `.env` 
- log files /
To prevent Git from tracking such files, we use a special file `.gitignore`.


**How to use it :**
- Create a file named `.gitignore`.
- Add names of files/folders you want to ignore.

Using `.gitignore` is important because it keeps your repository clean, avoids accidental commits of sensitive or heavy files.

pages.title: Git Commands for Undoing Changes
pages.content:
Git provides several commands that help you safely undo mistakes — \
whether it's **reverting a file, un-staging something, or even undoing a commit**. \
Let's see these git commands one by one :

---

**a) Undo changes in the working directory (discard edits)** \
Sometimes you change a file and then realise - \
**“I don’t want these edits at all. I want the file exactly how it was before.”**

**Git Command:**
```bash
git restore 
```

**What this command does**:
- Replaces your file with the last committed version.
- All your uncommitted edits are removed.
- You cannot get those discarded edits back.

pages.title: Unstage a file (when you added it by mistake)
pages.content:
Sometimes you run `git add ` and then realise - \
**“Wrong file added in staging area”**. \
In that case, **you can remove the file from the staging area without losing your changes**.

---

**Git Command:**
```bash
git restore --staged 
```

---

**What this command does**:
- Removes the file from staging → it won’t be part of the next commit.
- Keeps your changes safe → your edited file in the working directory stays exactly the same.
- Only the staging area is cleaned, nothing is deleted.

pages.title: Undo the last commit but keep your changes
pages.content:
Sometimes you make a commit and then realise: **“You committed too early!”** or \
**“I need to fix the message or add more changes.”**

In this case, you don’t want to lose your code — you only want to **remove the commit**, not your work.

---

**Git Command:**
```bash
git reset --soft HEAD~1
```

---

**What this command does**:
- Removes the latest commit from history.
- Moves all the commit’s changes back to the staging area.
- Your code is completely safe — **nothing is deleted**.
- In simple terms, this command **undoes your last commit without losing any work**.

**Breakdown of the command**:
- `git reset` → go back to an earlier commit
- `--soft` → keep all changes staged (safe)
- `HEAD` → your current commit
- `~1` → one commit back

pages.title: Undo the last commit and delete your changes
pages.content:
Sometimes you don’t need the last commit at all — \
you want to completely remove it **along with the changes made in it**.

---

**Git Command:**
```bash
git reset --hard HEAD~1
```

---


**What this command does:**
- Removes the latest commit from history.
- Deletes all the changes from that commit.
- Also removes those edits from your working files.
- This cannot be easily recovered, so use carefully.
- In simple terms, this command **undoes your last commit and deletes all associated changes permanently**.

**Breakdown of the command:**
- `git reset` → go back to an earlier commit
- `--hard` → remove changes from staging area and working directory (dangerous)
- `HEAD` → your current commit
- `~1` → one commit back

modules.description: In this module, you’ll explore GitHub, the platform that brings your Git projects online. You’ll learn what GitHub is, how it differs from Git, how to set up your github account, and how to create and manage repositories. By the end, you’ll be able to connect your local work to GitHub and confidently manage your projects online.

pages.title: Getting Started with GitHub
pages.content:
You’ve learned **the basics of Git** — how to save changes, create branches, and fix mistakes locally on your computer. \
Now it’s time to put your project online so you can store it safely, share it, and work with others. \
**That’s what GitHub is used for.**

---

**What is GitHub?** \
GitHub is a **website where you can store your Git Repositories online**. \
It’s like a cloud storage platform specially built for developers. \
**With GitHub, you can**:
- Keep your projects backed up safely
- Access them from anywhere
- Collaborate with others on your project


---

**How GitHub Differs From Git :** 
- **Git = Local tool** \
You use it on your computer to **track changes and manage your project’s history**.

- **GitHub = Online platform** \
It **stores your Git projects on the internet** and lets you **collaborate** through features like Pull Requests, Issues, and easy project sharing.

---
To start using GitHub, you need just one thing - **A GitHub account** \
Next, we’ll learn how to create your GitHub account step by step.

A Github Repository (Remote Repository) is a **project folder on GitHub.** \
A repo is a storage space that keeps your **project files, commits, and branches** all in one place.

- Public → Anyone can see your repo
- Private → Only you (and people you invite) can see it

This automatically creates your first file and makes the repo easier to understand. \
(You can skip `.gitignore` and `license` for now.)

pages.title: Add Remote
pages.content:
You just saw how a local project gets connected to GitHub. \
Now let’s break down each step used in that demo so everything becomes clear to you.

---

**Github Command** 
```bash
git remote add origin 
```

---

**How `git remote add origin ` Works :** \
When you run this command, you are basically telling Git: \
**“This is the GitHub repository where I want to store and push my project.”** \
Here’s what happens step-by-step:

**1. git remote add** \
You are adding a new remote connection (a link to an online repo). \
**2. origin** \
This is just a name Git uses for that connection. \
Instead of typing the long GitHub URL every time, you can simply say “origin”. \
**3. ``** \
This is the actual URL of your GitHub repository. \
Git saves this link internally so it knows where to push or pull from. \
**4. After the command** \
Your local Git project now knows which GitHub repo it belongs to. \
Git can now send (push) or receive (pull) data to/from that GitHub repo.

callout.text: GitHub hosts repositories remotely; remotes, pushes, pulls, and fetches coordinate local history with the remote repository.

pages.title: Setting the Correct Branch Name
pages.content:
Now that your local project is connected to GitHub, the next step is to make sure both sides use the same default branch name.

This ensures smooth syncing and avoids branch mismatches.

---

**Github Command:**
```bash
git branch -M main
```

---

**How `git branch -M main` Works** \
When you run this command, you are telling Git: \
**“Rename my current branch to main, no matter what its old name was.”** \
Here’s what happens step-by-step:

**1. git branch** \
This is the Git command used to create, view, or rename branches. \
**2. -M** \
`-M` forces the branch to be renamed to `main`, even if a branch with that name already exists. \
Replace any old main branch with the new one. \
**3. main** \
This becomes the new name of your current branch.

pages.title: Push Code to GitHub for the First Time
pages.content:
Your project is now linked to GitHub, and your branch name is set correctly. The final step is to push your code for the first time.

This is when your local files finally appear in your GitHub repository.

---

**Github Command:**
```bash
git push -u origin main
```

---

**How `git push -u origin main` Works** \
When you run this command, you are telling Git: \
**“Upload my local main branch to GitHub and remember this connection for next time.”** \
Here’s what happens step-by-step:

**1. git push** \
This sends your local commits (your code changes) to GitHub. 

**2. origin** \
This is the remote name you set earlier using: \
`git remote add origin ` \
It tells Git **where to push** — to your GitHub repository. 

**3. main** \
This is the branch you are pushing. \
You are saying: \
**“Send my local `main` branch → GitHub `main` branch.”**

**4. `-u` (set upstream)** \
It means: \
**“Git, remember this branch connection.”** \
For future push, just run:
```bash
git push
```
Git already knows where and what to push.

pages.title: Pulling updates (git pull)
pages.content:
Before continuing your work, your **local repo must stay updated with what’s on GitHub** and **in sync with others’ changes**. \
This module teaches you **how to bring the latest updates from `GitHub → your computer`**.

**Why Syncing Matters :**
- Avoids conflicts
- Prevents overwriting
- Keeps your project up-to-date 

And this is where **`git pull` comes in** — it downloads and merges the latest changes into your local repo.

---

**What is `git pull` ?** \
`git pull` is the command that **brings the latest changes** from **GitHub → your local machine** and **merges** them into your **current branch**.

In simple terms:
- It downloads changes
- It merges them into your local work
- Keeps you in sync with others

**Git Command**
```bash
git pull 
```

This pulls the latest updates from the **main** branch on GitHub into your **local main** branch.

---

**Now that you’ve learned `git push` and `git pull`, let’s visualize the difference to understand it clearly.** \

Push sends your changes to GitHub, while pull brings others’ changes from GitHub to you.

---

**Fun Fact** \
If you run `git pull` while your local branch has uncommitted changes that conflict with incoming remote changes, \
**Git will stop the pull** and **ask you to commit/stash** your local changes first.

- **Why?** \
Git wants to protect your local work from being accidentally overwritten

pages.title: Introduction to Git Fetch
pages.content:
Imagine you and your teammate are working on the same repo. Your teammate pushed some changes to GitHub, but **you don’t want to merge them into your branch** for now.

If you do:
```bash
git pull
```
**Git will fetch and merge automatically**.

- But sometimes you just want to **see what changed before merging**. \
**This is where `git fetch` comes in**.

---

**What git fetch does** 
- `git fetch` **downloads all the new commits from the remote**, but **does not merge** them into your branch.
- It **updates your local copy of the remote branch** (`origin/main`) without touching your current branch.
```bash
git fetch origin
```

---

**After fetching, you can check what changed**:
```bash
git log origin/main
```
This shows **All remote commits**.

- Another way for comparison :
```bash
git log main..origin/main
``` 
This shows **only the new commits you don’t have locally**.

---

And **merge manually** when you’re ready:
```bash
git merge origin/main
```

---

**Now that you understand both `git pull` and `git fetch`, let’s visualize the difference.** 

git pull fetches and merges automatically, while git fetch only downloads updates without merging them.

pages.title: Pushing Branches to GitHub
pages.content:
So far, you’ve learned how to create branches locally and on GitHub, and how to switch between them. Now, it’s time to share your work on a branch with others by **pushing it to GitHub**.

**GitHub Command to Push a Branch**
```bash
git push -u origin branch-name
```
**Explanation**:
- `git push` → Sends your branch commits to GitHub.
- `-u` → Sets the upstream branch, so future pushes are simpler (git push only).
- `origin` → Name of the remote repository.
- `branch-name` → The branch you want to push.

---

**Quick Steps: Pushing a Branch to GitHub**
1. **Switch** to your branch
```bash
git checkout branch-name
```
2. **Push** the branch to GitHub
```bash
git push -u origin branch-name
```
3. **Verify** online – your branch now appears in your GitHub repo.

Next time, just use `git push` for updates on the same branch.

pages.title: Pulling Latest Changes on a Branch
pages.content:
So far, you’ve learned how to push your branch to GitHub and make it available online.
Now, it’s equally important to **bring the latest updates from GitHub into your branch**, especially when your teammates have made changes.
This ensures your branch stays up-to-date and avoids conflicts later.

**GitHub Command to Pull Latest Changes**
```bash
git pull origin branch-name
```
**Explanation**:
- `git pull` → Downloads new changes AND merges them into your current branch.
- `origin` → Remote repository you are pulling from.
- `branch-name` → The branch you want to update with the latest changes.

---

**Quick Steps: Pulling Latest Changes on a Branch**

1. **Switch** to the branch you want to update
```bash
git checkout branch-name
```
2. **Pull** the latest updates from GitHub
```bash
git pull origin branch-name
```
3. **Check** your files – the newest changes from GitHub are now added to your branch.

modules.description: In this module, you’ll learn how Git and GitHub work in real projects, how to pull updates, use branches, and keep your local code synced with GitHub. You’ll also understand cloning and forking and when to use each. By the end, you’ll be ready to collaborate smoothly using both tools.

pages.title: Cloning a GitHub Repository
pages.content:
Before now, you created your own local repo → then connected it → then pushed. \
But in real projects, most of the time **the repository already exists on GitHub**, created by someone else.

So instead of making a repo from scratch, you simply download (copy) it to your system. Let's dive into this.

---

**What is Cloning?**
- **Downloading a full GitHub repository** into your **local machine**.
- Includes all **files, history, branches, commit logs**
- Automatically sets `remote = origin` i.e
Your local project is now linked to the GitHub repo(remote) you cloned, and that connection is called origin.
- No need for `git init` or `git remote add origin`

---

**Git Command to clone a repo**:
```bash
git clone 
```
**Example:**
```bash
git clone https://github.com/username/project-name.git
```

After this, a new folder is created and you're ready to start working on the project.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Cloning creates a local working copy; forking creates a separate GitHub repository under another account for independent collaboration.

It requires every change to be committed directly to the default branch before review.

pages.title: When Cloning Is Not Enough
pages.content:
You've learned how to clone a GitHub repository. \
Cloning works great when:
- the repo belongs to you, or
- you have permission to push to it. 
But now imagine this situation:

---

You find an amazing open-source project on GitHub: \
**“Recipe-Collection”** created by another developer. 

You want to: **add a new recipe** \
So you think: \
“Let me clone it and push my changes!”

**You clone it:**
```aaa
git clone https://github.com/someone/recipe-collection.git
```
You make your edits and **then try to push:**
```bash
git push
```
**And GitHub says:**

 **ERROR: Permission denied. You cannot push to this repository**.

Because… \
You are not the owner. You **don’t have write access**.

---

**This is where Forking comes in** \
When you don’t have permission to push to a repo, you create your own copy of it on your GitHub account.

Meaning:
- You get **full control over your fork**.
- You can **push your changes freely**.
- Later, you can **send a pull request to the owner**.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Cloning creates a local working copy; forking creates a separate GitHub repository under another account for independent collaboration.

pages.title: Forking a GitHub Repository
pages.content:
Forking means creating your own copy of someone else’s repository on GitHub so you can make changes without affecting the original project.

After forking, you clone your fork to your local machine to work on it.

---

**Fork on GitHub** 
1. **Go to the original repo** \
(Use this repo you used previously to clone : https://github.com/codechef8899/clone-practice-repo/) 


2. **Click the Fork button** → now the repo appears under your GitHub account

---

- Now you can clone your fork using `Git Clone`
- This creates a local copy of your fork

**You can now make changes, commit, and push freely to your fork**

Now that you understand repositories, branches, pushing, pulling, and forking… it’s time to learn **how real teams actually work together on GitHub**. \
When multiple developers work on the same project, everyone creates changes on their own branches. \

**This is where Pull Requests (PRs) come in.**

A Pull Request (PR) is how developers share their changes and ask for them to be added into the main project.

pages.title: Git Stash
pages.content:
You’ve now learned how to work with repositories, branches, PRs, and collaboration.
As you start working on real projects, you’ll often be in the middle of some changes—but not ready to commit them. \
At the same time, you may need to:
- switch to another branch,
- pull the latest updates, or
- fix something quickly. 

But Git won’t allow you to switch branches with unfinished changes. \
**This is where Git Stash helps**.

---

**What Git Stash Does** \
Git Stash **saves your unfinished changes temporarily**, so you can **switch branches safely** without losing anything. \
It stores your current work in a temporary safe place and **gives you a clean working directory** to continue working.

---

**Why It’s Useful**
- You don’t want to commit half-done code
- You need a clean working folder
- You must quickly move to another branch
- You want to come back and continue later

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Stash temporarily saves unfinished working-tree changes; rebase reapplies commits on a new base to keep a linear history.

pages.title: Saving Your Unfinished Work (Git Stash)

If you need to switch branches or pull updates, Git won’t let you unless your changes are saved or removed. \
Git Stash lets you save your work temporarily without committing it.

---

**Git Commands:**
```bash
git stash
```
This **saves all your `modified + staged` files temporarily**.

---

```bash
git stash push -m "message"
```
This **saves your changes with a message** so you can recognize them later. (Recommended)

pages.title: Applying Your Saved Work (Git Stash Apply)
pages.content:
You’ve learned how to save your unfinished changes using `Git Stash`. \
Now it’s time to **bring those saved changes back into your working directory**. \
For this, Git gives you the `apply` command.

---

**Git Commands:**

```bash
git stash apply
```
**Applies (restores) the latest stash** you saved.

---

```bash
git stash apply stash@{n}
```
**Applies a specific stash** from your stash list.

here, `n` represents the stash number (index) in your stash list. \
Git stores stashes in order, like a stack: 
- `stash@{0}` → the most recent stash
- `stash@{1}` → the second-most recent stash
- `stash@{2}` → the third-most recent stash
…and so on.

---

Both commands bring your changes back, but **they do NOT delete the stash** from the stash list — **they only restore the changes**.

callout.text: Stash temporarily saves unfinished working-tree changes; rebase reapplies commits on a new base to keep a linear history.

pages.title: Removing Stashes
pages.content:
When you no longer need your saved stashes, **Git allows you to remove them**. \
This helps keep your **stash list clean** and avoids confusion, especially when multiple stashes pile up. \
**You can remove one stash, remove a specific stash, or delete all of them at once**.

---

**1. Apply and Delete the Latest Stash** \
**Use when**: \
You want to restore your changes and automatically remove the stash.

**Command:**
```bash
git stash pop
```

---

**2. Delete a Specific Stash** \
**Use when**: \
You want to remove only one stash from the list.

**Command:**
```bash
git stash drop stash@{n}
```

---

**3. Delete All Stashes** \
**Use when**: \
You want to completely clean your stash history.

**Command:**
```bash
git stash clear
```

pages.title: Git Rebase
pages.content:
You’ve learned how `git stash` helps keep your workspace clean. \
Now let’s look at another tool that **keeps your commit history clean — `Git Rebase`**.

Rebase may sound advanced, but the core idea is simple: \
it **rearranges your commits so your branch history becomes clean, linear, and easy to understand**.

---

**What Is Git Rebase?** \
git rebase takes the commits from your branch and replays them on top of the latest commits from another branch — usually `master` — so your branch becomes updated and the history looks clean.


---

**Git Command**
```bash
git rebase master
```

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Stash temporarily saves unfinished working-tree changes; rebase reapplies commits on a new base to keep a linear history.

pages.title: Understanding Git Rebase from Simple Example
pages.content:
- You’re working on `feature` branch.
- New commits appear in `master`.
- Your branch is now behind.
- You run:
```bash
git checkout feature
git rebase master
```
This makes your `feature` branch look like it was created from the newest version of `master`, \
as if your work started after all the new commits on `master`.

---

**Note :** 
- **If conflicts happen during a rebase, fix them manually in the files, then run**:
```bash
git rebase --continue
```
This continues the rebase.

- **If the rebase is too messy, has too many conflicts, or you decide not to apply the changes**. \
Then **to cancel an ongoing rebase** and return to the branch’s previous state, use:
```bash
git rebase --abort
```

pages.title: Git Cherry-Pick
pages.content:
Imagine you are working on your project in the `main` branch. \
A teammate has **fixed a small bug in the `feature`** branch, but the **rest of that branch is not ready yet**. \
You **don’t want to merge the entire `feature`** branch, but you do **want that specific bug fix** in your branch.

This is exactly when **Git cherry-pick** comes in handy. 

---

**What Is Git Cherry-Pick ?** \
A **tool that lets you one or more specific commits from one branch and apply them to another** without merging the whole branch. 


---

**Git Command :**
```bash
git cherry-pick 
```

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Cherry-pick copies one selected commit onto the current branch without merging the entire source branch.

pages.title: Understanding Git Cherry-Pick from Simple Example
pages.content:
**Scenario:**
You have two branches: `main` and `feature`.

The feature branch has three commits:
1. Commit `2a` – some changes
2. Commit `2b` – a bug fix you need in `main`
3. Commit `2c` – work not ready yet

You **don’t want to merge the whole feature branch** — only the **specific commit** `2b`. 
- Let's Understand this Visually :

**Solution**: \
Use **Git cherry-pick** to apply just that commit to `main`.

**Git Commands:**
```bash
git checkout main - Switch to main branch
git cherry-pick - Apply the specific commit from feature branch
```

---

**Note :**
- If conflicts appear, fix them, then continue:
```bash
git cherry-pick --continue
```
- To cancel cherry-pick anytime:
```bash
git cherry-pick --abort
```
